title: FCC Review of E-Rate Program Sparks Fears of Internet Funding Cuts for Schools
summary: A federal program that has connected nearly every U.S. school and library to the internet is under review, and educators are on edge. The E-Rate program, created by Congress in 1996, provides discounted internet access to schools and libraries. It's widely credited with helping boost internet connectivity from 14% of schools to near 100%. But the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) announced a full review in late June, and some fear it's a prelude to cuts. David Thurston, who oversees technology for 33 school districts in California's sprawling San Bernardino County, says E-Rate covers tens of thousands of dollars in monthly internet bills. "There's no doing without," he said. "School districts are gonna have to pick up the costs." The review has puzzled many because, as Thurston notes, "by its own data and its own measurement, the program is healthy." FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, who helped write a section of the conservative Project 2025 blueprint targeting broadband spending, has cited children's screen time as a key reason for the review. The FCC's notice of proposed rulemaking calls for measures "to better protect children when using E-Rate-funded networks, including to limit screen time." Several states have recently passed laws restricting technology in classrooms, and the Los Angeles Unified School District approved a screen-time policy. But advocates argue that gutting E-Rate is the wrong approach. "We believe there are ways of strengthening school policies to promote more limited and privacy-protecting use of EdTech without taking away critical E-Rate funding," said Josh Golin of Fairplay. Schools depend on the internet for attendance, bus routing, and online testing—48 states now administer exams online. Bob Bocher of the American Library Association says the FCC likely cannot eliminate E-Rate because it's enshrined in the Telecommunications Act of 1996, and the Supreme Court recently upheld the funding mechanism. But the agency could make the program so burdensome that schools and libraries abandon it, effectively achieving the same result.
why_it_matters: If the E-Rate program is weakened, students in low-income school districts could lose the internet access that makes modern education possible—from homework help to college-prep tests. The review also shows how a single agency's rulemaking can reshape a tool that nearly every U.S. student relies on, raising big questions about who decides what's best for kids.

background_read: The E-Rate program was created by the Telecommunications Act of 1996 to ensure that schools and libraries, especially in poor and rural areas, could afford internet access. It is funded through fees paid by telecommunications companies, a method the U.S. Supreme Court recently upheld.

FCC Chairman Brendan Carr previously helped write a section of Project 2025, a conservative policy roadmap for a future Republican administration, that specifically targets broadband spending and questions the value of universal service funds. His mention of screen time taps into growing concerns about technology in classrooms, which several states and the large Los Angeles Unified School District have addressed with new restrictions.

The American Library Association and groups like Fairplay worry that the FCC could use the review to pile on so many rules and requirements that schools give up on the program, even if they can't legally eliminate it. Because nearly every U.S. school now relies on E-Rate for everything from online testing to bus routing, any funding reduction could widen the digital divide.

perspectives.description: Screen time concerns are legitimate; excessive use of devices in schools can harm concentration and mental health. A review that encourages healthier technology habits without cutting funding could lead to better educational outcomes and protect children from overexposure.

Critics see the screen time argument as a cover for dismantling a successful program that conservative blueprints have long targeted. If E-Rate is gutted, the financial burden would fall directly on school districts, forcing cuts in other areas or leaving low-income students without reliable internet.

The E-Rate debate mirrors a larger tension: as schools become more tech-dependent, regulating that technology becomes both a health issue and a political battleground. The FCC's authority to review the program is legal, but using it to impose ideological preferences sets a precedent for how federal agencies can subtly reshape long-standing laws.

If the FCC adds heavy bureaucracy, many schools may silently drop out of E-Rate, creating a two-tier system where affluent districts pay for their own internet and others fall behind. Advocates are likely to challenge any drastic changes in court, arguing they violate the program's original purpose, so the outcome could redefine digital equity for a generation.
